tagline.text: A forest and grassland hike that starts by the sea next to Laiya Beach

location.label: Location
location.text: Brgy. Hugom, San Juan, Batangas (between San Juan and Lobo)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Day hike to 2 days and 1 night

children.text: Mount Daguldol is a coastal mountain of about 670 m that starts from Barangay Hugom in San Juan, Batangas. The trail runs from rocky shoreline through forest to grassland, and you can rest at Laiya Beach afterward, which makes it popular as both a day hike and an overnight trip.
Mount Daguldol (also spelled Daguldul) is a coastal mountain between San Juan and Lobo in Batangas. It stands about
(672 m in some sources), and the jump-off is near the beach in Barangay Hugom, San Juan. Hiking sites classify it as a difficulty 3/9 "minor climb" with trail class 1–3. From Manila it takes about
4 hours
by road, so a day hike requires a pre-dawn start.

The route falls into three parts. You first walk along the shore past rock formations, then enter forest trail, and finally climb onto a windy grassland ridge. According to guides, the early stretch is flat concrete road and a gentle slope, and the middle passes a stream, coconut groves, grazing livestock and rocky outcrops. The total trail length is described as about
9 km
About halfway there is a rest stop known as "Mang Lizardo's place." Older reports say it sold simple food, soft drinks, coconut juice and honey. From there it is another
1.5–2 hours
up to the campsite near the summit. Campsites mentioned include Niyugan (with coconut trees), Anahawan and the Gulugod Baboy campsite, and Niyugan is said to be the only water source.

The summit is a windy meadow with some rock, and some guides say the views are not especially spectacular. Even so, reports mention seeing far-off mountains such as Mindoro, Mount Banahaw, Mount Cristobal, Mount Banoi and Naguiling Peak on clear days, and a viewpoint about
20 minutes

from the Niyugan campsite is said to overlook Maculot, Malipunyo, Tayabas Bay and Marinduque. The actual view depends on the weather, so keep your expectations modest and treat this as a hike that combines forest and shoreline.

blocks.title: A hike that starts at the beach

children.text: The jump-off is near the beach, so the first part of the hike is sea and rock formations. Soon you enter the forest, and the change of scenery from sea to mountain is the character of this hike.

The middle section is a forest trail that passes a stream and coconut fields. Reports say that in harvest season coconut husks lie on the trail and locals sometimes offer fresh coconut. There is a lot of livestock dung, so watch your step.
Often mentioned in older reports as a midway rest area, it reportedly sold simple food, coconut juice and honey. It is not confirmed that it still operates this way, so bring your own food.

Reports say the summit has a wide meadow where many tents fit. One report says the land above the campsite is privately owned but open to hikers, and another says the campsite is not the summit itself and the real summit is about
25 minutes
farther.
A viewpoint about
20 minutes
from the Niyugan campsite, described as overlooking Maculot, Malipunyo, Banahaw, Mindoro, Tayabas Bay and Marinduque.
A waterfall of about 25 m roughly
5 minutes
off the trail. One report says it flows only in the June–October wet season and is dry in summer, so check before you go.
Many hikers watch the sunset and swim at Laiya Beach after the descent. It is described as about
35 minutes
by vehicle from the Hugom jump-off. Resort fees and beach access rules differ by resort, so check locally.
Some hikers also climb Mt. Hugom (about 570 m) as a day hike from the same jump-off. If Daguldol is not enough, you could plan it as a follow-up.

items.title: Day hike from Manila
items.subtitle: Dawn start, Laiya Beach in the afternoon

children.text: Leave Manila for San Juan. One report left Cubao at 2 a.m. and reached the jump-off in about
4 hours
Register at the Hugom jump-off, find a guide and have breakfast.
Start hiking. You climb through beach, forest and grassland in that order.
Reach the upper area, take photos and eat lunch. One reported itinerary reached the summit area at this time.
Begin the descent. The grassland section has little wind and can be very hot.
Return to the jump-off, rest, and head to Laiya Beach.
Leave for Manila. Some reports say transport out of Laiya stops early in the evening, so hurry your return.
Hiking pace varies a lot from person to person. One report reached the summit in about
4 hours
and took about
8 hours
round trip. Leave generous time for resting at Laiya Beach afterward.
Take a Lipa-bound bus from Buendia or Cubao.
Register at Hugom, find a guide and have lunch.
Start hiking. Pass Mang Lizardo's rest stop and climb to the campsite.
Reach the campsite, pitch your tent and have dinner.
Get up and watch the sunrise from the summit. In bad weather a dawn climb is difficult.
Descend to Hugom and relax at Laiya Beach.

One report says a day tour from Manila left before dawn and took about
4 hours
to reach the jump-off. What is included varies by operator.
Hugom to Laiya Beach is described as about
35 minutes
by van. Ask your guide or the village about transport to the beach after the hike.
The dry season from November to May is the best time to climb. The summit is more likely to be clear and the trail less slippery. In March–May, however, the grassland and the descent are very hot.
During the June–October wet season the trail is slippery. Naambon Falls flows then, but some reports say night hikes or camping can be blocked by weather.
This is a mountain where the pace tends to slow, so for a day hike, leaving early is the most important thing.

Summit views depend heavily on season and weather. In the dry season far-off mountains are more likely to show, while in the wet season cloud hides them and the forest and waterfall become the attraction. In any season, leaving early and avoiding midday is best.

items.label: Guide (day hike)
items.note: Hugom Environmental Guides Association; check locally

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.

There are small guesthouses near Hugom village and the beach, and Laiya Beach has a cluster of resorts that make a good place to stay after the hike. Prices vary widely by resort and date, so check booking sites. If you camp, ask your guide first about the campsite and whether water is available at Niyugan.

It is safest to assume you cannot buy food on the mountain. Older reports mention a midway stop selling food and drinks, but it is not confirmed that it still operates. Bring water and lunch. Some reports mention going for Batangas' famous lomi after the hike. If you want a shower and lunch at the beach, ask the resort about fees first.
Laiya Beach resorts reportedly charge different beach-use and shower fees. An older report lists resort use at about
per person, and another says even just bathing at a resort beach can cost extra. Laiya is about
35 minutes
by vehicle after the hike, but there are reports that evening transport stops early, so decide your ride home or your lodging in advance. One guide listed an estimated total budget of about
including the guide (an older figure); prices may have risen, so budget extra.
For a day hike, leave at dawn. You avoid the strong sun and reach Laiya Beach earlier.
Bring
2–3 liters
of water. Prepare lunch and snacks in advance and carry your trash out.
Pack swimwear and a towel so you can go straight into the sea at Laiya Beach after the hike.
A guide is required. Parts of the trail are confusing, so always go with a guide.
Bring sunscreen, a hat, an umbrella or raincoat and comfortable hiking shoes.
Phone signal reaches some sections and the summit, but it varies by section. Bring a power bank.
Reports say transport out of Laiya stops early in the evening, so decide your return time in advance.
For camping, bring a waterproof tent, flashlight, jacket and insect repellent.
Reports on leeches are mixed. One older guide says leeches have retreated deep into the range, while other reports say there are none. In the wet season, wear long socks and use repellent.
A night climb may be hard because of weather. For an overnight trip, a safer plan is to climb in daylight and watch the sunrise from the campsite.
Many reports and fees date from 2011–2018. Check the latest guide rules, fees and camping availability at the Hugom village registration desk.
Do not climb without a guide; parts of the trail are confusing.
The grassland and the descent have little shade and are hot. Watch for heat stroke.
In the wet season the trail is slippery and night hikes can be blocked by weather.
Some reports say certain resorts restrict hikers from passing their property or charge extra for beach use. Check beforehand.
Some sections have a lot of livestock dung. Watch your step.
A beach about
35 minutes
by vehicle from the Hugom jump-off, good for resting and watching the sunset after the hike.
A waterfall of about
by the trail; reports say it flows only in the June–October wet season. It is dry in the dry season, so check.
A mountain of about 570 m climbed as a day hike from the same Hugom jump-off. Worth considering if you have time and energy left.
A traverse combined with Daguldol has been reported, but reports also say the Hugom guides may not know the route. Ask your guide in advance.
